newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland's Orange Order's roots in ancient war.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland's Orange Order's roots in ancient war.

text.p: The Orange Order, whose Portadown parade has led to an ugly stand-off between Catholic residents and security forces, is rooted in ancient religious wars between Protestant and Catholic leaders.

Its name comes from Dutch King William of Orange, who vanquished Catholic King James's forces at the battle of the River Boyne on July 12, 1690, a victory which ensured that a Protestant ascended to the British throne.
That victory is marked on the "Glorious Twelfth," a yearly celebration which climaxes the Orange Order's annual marching season, involving about 2,500 parades.

Most go unnoticed and unchallenged. But in recent years Northern Ireland Catholics have formed residents' groups to object to parades through areas where they live, branding the marches sectarian, triumphalist and intimidatory.

The Order is not confined to Northern Ireland. It has branches in Scotland and the Irish Republic, where the organisation staged a totally peaceful parade on Saturday, as it has done for decades. It also has lodges in Canada and New Zealand.
The Orange Order, which has 80,000 members in Northern Ireland, says the parades are peaceful celebrations and that it is Catholic protest that has turned them into confrontations.
Many of Northern Ireland's political leaders, including David Trimble, head of the Ulster Unionist Party, the province's biggest pro-British grouping, are Orange Order members.

Members parade in Sunday-best dark suits and bowler hats in a nod towards the British way of life they cherish in the enclave of Northern Ireland, which Britain created when it partitioned the island of Ireland seven decades ago.
Protestants believe their religion would be suppressed if Northern Ireland were merged with the neighbouring 95 percent Catholic Ireland.
The Protestant catch cries "No Surrender" and "Not An Inch" are timeless mottos of a diehard will to guard a British foothold carved by colonist ancestors in Ireland.

Heraldic regalia, orange sashes, pipe bands and ceremonial swords are part of its paraphernalia, but Catholics say the organisation is a sinister reminder of ancient conflict that has no place in the 20th century island of Ireland.
Brandishing British flags, silver swords and pikes, wearing gleaming white gloves and armlets, the Orange Order marches down what it calls "the Queen's highway" with banners flying.
Catholic Irish Nationalists complain of swaggering Orangemen intent on reviving Protestant supremacy. Orangemen reply they are just proud to be Protestant and British.

Formed during agrarian sectarian conflict between descendants of Protestant "planters" sent to Ireland from Britain and Catholic gangs who wanted their land back, the Order is the voice of Protestant resistance to political change.
Behind huge banners depicting biblical scenes and Protestant triumphs, they march to laud politico-religious Britishness that pluralist Britain buried generations ago.
The Orange Order's network of "lodges" stood out against London plans 90 years ago to give Ireland internal home-rule.
"Home Rule is Rome Rule", its leaders declaimed before partition in 1922 liberated the republic and kept the north British, an act that Irish-born Catholics resent to this day.
Ever since, Northern Ireland's Catholic minority has branded it a dark force that has fomented sectarianism and that ensured one-sided Protestant control until Britain enforced reforms 25 years ago.
